correctness.rationale: The finite subset-sum recurrence is proved by the disjoint inclusion-or-omission cases for each divisor. Packed exact arbitrary-precision integer bitsets enumerate all sums from 0 to n! for n=1..12, with no heuristic cutoff. At 12!, the 7-term complement has 175 bits, first at 475785157, while eight terms cover all 479001601 possible totals. Independent divisor generation and a permuted-order traversal agree; direct set-based brute force agrees through n=5; an explicit eight-divisor witness is checked.

evidence: Hughes establishes h(n!) <= (2 log 2+o(1))n/log n, and a logarithmic-squared order lower bound, neither of which specializes to the precise n=12 value.
Tenenbaum–Yokota 1990 Lemma 4 holds for all sufficiently large k with an unspecified threshold and an asymptotic term bound, not an exact minimum.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The verified general theorems do not imply h(12!)=8 or count the 175 witnesses. The earlier Yokota papers remain partial-access risks; no decisive full-text comparison is claimed for them.

originality.rationale: The same-object Hughes 2026 paper proves an asymptotic upper bound and cites a qualitative counting lower bound, but supplies no exact initial factorial profile or maximal-length census. Tenenbaum–Yokota 1990, Lemma 4 likewise treats sufficiently large factorials and asymptotic term bounds. The exact 12! value, first eight-term threshold and 175-case census were not present in checked published-finding corpus hits, published-index/sequence searches, or the two current/prior own ledgers. Earlier Yokota full texts were inaccessible and are recorded as access risks rather than assumed not to cover.
residual_risks: The full texts of Yokota (1992) and Yokota (1995) were unavailable despite bounded lawful access attempts; an unindexed exact table in them cannot be ruled out.
The published-finding corpus semantic index and web searches are not exhaustive of unpublished or unindexed literature.
The theorem gives no asymptotic improvement and no classification for factorials with index greater than 12.

value.rationale: Erdős’s unresolved growth question for the natural invariant h(n!) motivates exact early-value benchmarks. The complete 1..12 initial profile determines the first new eight-term threshold, not an arbitrarily selected integer. The exceptionally thin 175-member maximal-length layer at 12! is a meaningful exact boundary for conjecturing exceptional-set behavior and evaluating constructive algorithms. This is a self-contained non-implied finite classification, not a generic computation of tau(n!) or a cosmetic numeric improvement.
